en: The *Huayan Wujiao Zhiguan* (The Cessation and Contemplation of the Five Teachings of the Avatamsaka),
spoken by Du Shun— an emanation of Mañjuśrī at Mount Zhongnan in the capital—
presents five dharma-gates of cessation and contemplation for practitioners to cultivate the path, distinguishing the heterodox and entering the orthodox.

1. The Gate of the Existence of Dharmas and the Non-existence of Self: the Teaching of the Hīnayāna; 2. The Gate of Birth as Non-birth: the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna; 3. The Gate of the Perfect Interfusion of Phenomena and Principle: the Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna; 4. The Gate of the Simultaneous Cessation of Words and Contemplation: the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna; 5. The Gate of the Avataṃsaka Samādhi: the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle. Regarding the first, the Gate of the Existence of Dharmas and the Non-existence of Self: indeed, prescriptions are tailored to the specific ailment.
When the illness is exhausted, the remedy ceases;
when the grasping is treated, the medicine is administered;
once the grasping is dispelled, the medicine has finished its work.
Since illnesses are manifold,
the medicines prescribed are not uniform; thus,
the methods of cultivation differ according to individual capacities.
Therefore, the skillful means differ.
Now, focusing specifically on the five *śamatha-vipaśyanā* practices (*pañca-nīvaraṇa-pratipakṣa*),
[the Buddha] addresses those sentient beings who are attached to a self.
The contemplation on the analysis of the elements is taught:
since beginningless time, sentient beings have clung to the body as a single entity.
One calculates "self" and "what belongs to self.
Regarding the calculation of "self," there are two types:
first, the attachment to the body as the self.
Second is the abandonment of the attachment to a self within the body.
Regarding the phrase "abandoning the attachment to a self within the body," this refers to the non-Buddhists who calculate that there exists a distinct, divine self (ātman) within the body.
This has been refuted at length in the sūtras and śāstras;
I shall not further elaborate on it here with prolixity.
As for what is called "clinging to the body as the self":
The Tathāgata, out of compassion, holds that these afflictions must be eradicated;
therefore, he has fully revealed four medicines to treat four diseases.
Within these, each distinct category contains its own specific medicine and disease.
This is as explained in detail below.
Regarding the "four diseases," the first is to grasp the body as a single self.
Second, clinging to the four great elements;
third, clinging to the five aggregates;
fourth, clinging to the twelve bases.
Regarding the four medicines:
first, the two dharmas of form and mind;
second, the four great elements and the five aggregates.
The thirty-two bases (āyatana) and the forty-eight elements (dhātu) are these. Next,
the explanation follows.
If sentient beings become afflicted by grasping at the body as a single self,
then the two dharmas of form and mind are taught as the medicine.
It is also said:
Within this, there are indeed two dharmas: form and mind.
How could they constitute a single self?
Upon hearing this, sentient beings immediately turn their attachment toward form and mind, grasping them as real and thereby falling into error.
This immediately opens up a single form and immediately opens up a single mind.
Form consists of four forms;
these are the four great elements.
The single mind is opened into four minds;
these are precisely the four aggregates among the five aggregates.
These are thus the four forms and the four minds.
Why do they cling only to one form and one mind as a single self?
Furthermore, sentient beings then further cling to four forms and four minds, which becomes a sickness.
The Buddha then combines the four great elements into a single form for them.
This refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) among the five aggregates.
Combining the four mental aggregates into one constitutes the sense-base of mind (*mano-āyatana*) among the twelve sense-bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).
When sentient beings hear this, they again become attached to it, which becomes an affliction.
The Buddha then divides a single form into eleven forms.
As for what these eleven are:
That is to say, within the twelve bases (āyatana), the five internal sense organs and the six external objects constitute eleven categories of form (rūpa).
The single category of mind is divided into seven categories of mind.
These are precisely the six consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*).
Since these constitute the eighteen elements themselves,
how can you directly grasp a single form or a single mind as being a self?
Upon hearing this, sentient beings will awaken and thereby enter into emptiness.
Now, within each of the eighteen realms, there are three types:
namely, the internal realm, the external realm, and the intermediate realm.
Furthermore, within each of these three types, two categories are distinguished:
first, the three illnesses;
second, the three medicines.
Regarding the three types of illness:
the first is that which consists of grasping at the six internal sense bases as a self by way of their general characteristics.
Second, there are those who externally grasp the six sense objects as a whole and consider them to be "mine.
Third, there are those who collectively reckon the intermediate six consciousnesses [as such].
The general characteristic is that which constitutes the view of self;
that is to say, it is the notion: "I see," "I hear," "I perceive," and "I know.
Next, it says there are three kinds of medicine.
One portion consists of the six internal sense bases as the six elements;
these refer to the eye element and so forth.
This serves to remedy the previous affliction of conceiving a self.
Second, externally, the six sense objects are established as the six elements;
these refer to the element of form and so forth.
This serves to remedy the affliction of the prior conception of "mine."
The middle third consists of my seeing, hearing, and so forth, which are cognized by the six consciousnesses;
that is to say, the visual consciousness element, the auditory consciousness element, and so on.
These serve as the remedy for the aforementioned afflictions of my seeing, hearing, and so forth.
The above three points collectively clarify the distinctions in numerical designations, titles, and boundaries,
which differ between this and that.
Taken collectively as a topical outline, it is called the "Dharmas of the Eighteen Dhātus.
What is termed "dhātu" (element) means "distinctness.
"Eighteen" is the number.
Therefore, they are called the eighteen *dhātus*.
Within each of these aforementioned phenomena,
there are six layers.
First, name;
second, phenomenon;
third, essence.
Fourth is the characteristic;
fifth is the function;
sixth is the cause.
What is called "name" refers to that which speaks from within the eye-faculty and the mouth.
What is called "thing" refers to...
That which is designated by the name is that which corresponds to a single thought-moment and is like an illusion.
That which is called its "substance" refers to the eight subtle entities.
What are called the eight subtle elements (*aṇu*) are solidity,
moisture, warmth, motion, color, odor, taste, and tangibility.
As for what is called their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*):
The eye is like the flower of the *gandharva*;
it is also said to be like a cluster of grapes.
As for what is called its "function":
This refers to that which gives rise to visual consciousness.
Furthermore, there are four meanings:
first, visual consciousness acts as the eye-faculty.
Second, it gives rise to eye-consciousness;
third, eye-consciousness belongs to the eye-faculty;
fourth, it assists the eye-faculty. These are the [characteristics].
What is called the "cause" refers to the seeds of the root of the ālayavijñāna.
The ear-organ has the appearance of a slanting *bako* tree.
The nose faculty is like a covered fingernail;
the tongue faculty has the appearance of a curved moon-shaped blade;
the body faculty has the appearance of a snake poised upon the ground.
If based on the Hīnayāna,
it is like the appearance of a lotus;
if based on the Mahāyāna, [it is otherwise].
Its characteristic is that it arises simultaneously with the four afflictions.
These four afflictions are:
self-love, self-pride, self-delusion, and the view of self.
The essence of the mind-faculty (*manas*) is the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Its function is that which is designated as the object of expression by the term "mind," namely, that which internally takes a single moment of consciousness as its object and clings to it as a self.
Excluding the substance and function of the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*),
the remaining faculties may be understood by analogy with the eye-faculty.
As for the second category, the six external objects (*viṣaya*):
Each of these has six aspects.
First, "name" refers to the verbal expressions within speech; this is the aspect of form (rūpa).
Second, "referent" (artha) refers to that which is signified by the name—a single moment associated with visual consciousness; this is the aspect of matter (rūpa-dravya).
Third is that which constitutes the substance of the eight subtle elements;
fourth is that which constitutes the characteristics of blue, yellow, red, and white;
fifth is that which functions to induce the arising of visual consciousness.
The sixth is that which consists of the seeds of form within the ālayavijñāna; these are the seeds of form.
The sense-object of sound has as its characteristic sounds that are great or small, long or short.
The sense-object of fragrance has as its characteristic odors such as fragrant and foul.
The sense-object of taste has sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, and acrid as its characteristics.
The sense-object of touch has cold, heat, roughness, smoothness, hardness, softness, lightness, heaviness, and so forth as its characteristics.
The sense-object of mental phenomena (dharmas) has square, round, long, short, and other dimensions and measurements as its characteristics.
The dharma-object (dharmaviṣaya) has ignorance as its essence.
Apart from the essence of the dharma-object,
the remaining five objects should be understood by analogy with the object of form (rūpaviṣaya).
Regarding the six intermediate consciousnesses:
the first is that which is called the eye-consciousness of verbal expression within the mouth;
the second is that which is called the ineffable reality that cannot be fully conveyed by names, yet whose subtle attainment is not lost.
Regarding the three essences, their essence is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Regarding the four characteristics, their characteristic is purity and perfection.
Regarding the five functions, their function is the clear cognition of objects.
The six causes refer to the seeds of the visual consciousness within the ālayavijñāna.
However, regarding the "objects" within the mental consciousness (manovijñāna),
these are those designated by names that do not correspond with correct reasoning.
It takes all that is encountered as its object.
With the exception of the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
the other five consciousnesses should be understood in accordance with the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Since the six elements—name, object, and so forth—are each one realm, they total eighteen realms;
when combined with the [original] eighteen, they constitute one hundred and eight realms.
There are sutras that employ these as the one hundred and eight afflictions.
Just as it is with the diseases to be cured,
so too it is with the medicines that cure them;
both the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses alike take the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as their essence.
Thus, the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
"The ocean of the ālayavijñāna abides eternally,
yet it is stirred by the winds of objective realms."
"The waves of various consciousnesses constantly arise,
surging and evolving.
Based on this scriptural passage.
This is what can be realized.
If a practitioner contemplates these eighteen elements (dhātus),
they will sever the aforementioned afflictions.
One attains liberation from "self" and "what belongs to self.
This is precisely the mind capable of contemplation,
which is the object contemplated by wisdom.
The absence of a person means that one has attained the wisdom of non-self regarding persons.
Although the self of persons has departed,
attachment to phenomena still persists.
The grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) refers to form and mind (*rūpacitta*).
Question: What is the difference between this grasping at phenomena regarding form and mind and the previous refutation of the single self (*ātman*) and form-and-mind?
Answer: In the former case, there was a person based on a single body.
Therefore, by taking up matter and mind, he refutes [the notion of] views; thus,
through such successive unfolding, he expands a single body into eleven types of matter and a single mind into seven types of mind, and so forth.
Only upon reaching this point does one begin to know that [things] arise from the conjunction of various conditions.
Thus, although people perceive the beginning of death,
they have not yet clarified the principle through discernment.
They still cling to the various conditions as being truly existent;
such is their difference.
This concludes the brief exposition on the Small Vehicle’s refutation of the grasping at a self, and the explanation of the contemplation of the analysis of the elements is finished.
Regarding the second gate, "Arising is itself Non-arising": as for the gate "Arising is itself Non-arising," it means that...
Within this section,
first the names and characteristics are distinguished,
and subsequently one enters the gate of non-arising.
Now, first, regarding the distinction between name and characteristic:
for the time being, taking the worldly perspective,
one can identify them by selecting any single object.
For now, let us examine this upon a single pillow.
To ask without contradicting worldly convention:
what would you call it?
Answer: It is the pillow.
Question: What, then, is that?
Answer: It is the name.
He asked again,
"What is this pillow?
He replied, "It is a wooden pillow."
He asked again,
"And what is this wooden pillow?
He replied, "It is not a name."
He asked again:
"Since it is not a name,
what should it be called?"
This was his answer.
Again he asked,
"What do you call the pillow?"
The answer was, "It is not a phrase.
He asked again,
"Since it is not a phrase,"
"What is it called?
He replied, "It is named.
He asked again:
"What is the use of a 'named general'?
He replied, "A 'named general' is used for summoning affairs.
He asked again.
Sōzan said, “The pillow has arrived.
This refers to that which has already arrived.
What is this? To remain silent is not to require speech;
this is the answer by silence.
He asked again,
"What exactly is this?
He replied, "It is not a pillow."
He asked again:
"Since it is not a pillow,
where has the pillow gone?"
The answer was: "It is called 'name'.
He asked again:
"Where does name reside?"
The answer is: "It is that which is spoken with the mouth.
Again he asked:
"Since this is not a pillow..."
"What is it called?
He replied, "It is beyond words.
He asked again.
How is it known that [reality] is beyond words?
Answer: Because it is seen by the eye, it is conventionally expressed through words.
Again, he asked:
If it is designated by conventional verbal expressions, what thing is being called?
The answer is: "It is this matter."
He asked again:
"Matters are of many kinds;
some are matters of characteristics."
Is it a matter of form (rūpa), or a matter of principle (dharma)?
Answer: This is a matter of characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
He asked again: "Furthermore,
characteristics are also of many kinds,
such as the characteristics of being crooked, square, circular, and so forth."
Answer: This is the characteristic of direction.
Again he asked:
There are many kinds of characteristics of direction.
Regarding the term "of many kinds," it refers to the distinctness of shared purpose (*samānārthatā*).
The answer is that this is the name for the lower part of the pillow's appearance.
He asked again:
"Among the eight consciousnesses, to which mind are names, signs, and objects subsumed?
He replied: "Names, signs, and objects are subsumed within the sixth mental consciousness among the gates of the visual consciousness."
He asked again:
"From what source do these names, marks, and objects suddenly appear within the mind of the mental consciousness?
He replied: "They come from seeds."
Question: How is this known?
Answer: Because the characteristics (nāma-lakṣaṇa) of this pillow cannot be the characteristics of a mat, we know that it arises from seeds.
Question: From where is the seed obtained?
Answer: It is obtained from a false teacher.
Question again:
When it is attained, how is it attained?
Answer: Because seeds are formed through the熏 (xūn, perfuming) of seeing and hearing.
Again, he asked:
Since these names, marks, and objects already exist within the consciousness and mind,
one ought to look within the mind;
why then do you look outward before you?
Answer: When looking back at what preceded, these names and characteristics are entirely within the mind.
Again, he asked:
How is this known?
The answer is: visual consciousness merely perceives form;
names, characteristics, and entities reside within the mind of the mental consciousness.
He asked again:
"I, a deluded person, see only names and marks;
you, a wise one who has seen form—what do you see?"
"What are their characteristics? What is form?
He then asked the deluded person in return.
"You see names and forms;
what are their characteristics?
The deluded person replied:
"One who has four edges and six faces is a wise person.
He asked,
"Look at the direction of the edges."
"When you see it, do you see the edge or do you see the color?
When the deluded person carefully observes and answers, they say:
"I see only the color; I do not see the edge."
The same questions and answers apply to the other facets as well.
A deluded person asked:
"If it is entirely composed of form (rūpa),..."
"Where do names and forms reside?
The wise man replied,
"Names and forms reside within your own mind."
The deluded person would not submit.
A wise man asked him,
"For what reason do you not submit?"
The deluded person replied,
"As I currently see the temple gate tower prophesied by the Buddha,
its name and appearance are what I have been looking at within my mind for some time."
The names and characteristics have likewise entered my mind.
For what reason does one person obtain them while another does not?
The wise man asked in return,
"Bring me the names and forms.
The deluded person replied:
"I have already obtained it.
The wise man asked,
"What have you obtained?"
The deluded person replied,
"I have grasped names and characteristics.
He asked again:
"Is this name-and-form soft or hard?
He replied, "It is hard.
The wise man said:
"Leave the hardness aside and grasp only the name and appearance;
do not grasp the hardness itself.
The deluded person replied:
Both the physical hardness and the name-and-characteristics are obtained.
He asked again:
"Can one then see it?"
He replied, "I cannot see.
He was asked again,
"What do you see?"
Answer: One merely perceives names and appearances.
Yet, those who are deluded ask about them;
having grasped these names and appearances, they claim to have attained [realization].
[The questioner] asked, "If only names and appearances are grasped, where do they reside?
The wise person replied,
"Names and appearances reside within the minds of deluded people."
Deluded people do not submit;
names and forms remain within their minds.
A wise person asks:
"Why do you not submit?
The deluded person replied,
"Since all manner of names and characteristics are already within my own mind."
Why is it that one does not attain hardness uniformly?
Answer: One attains hardness.
If one attains hardness, [then...]
This refers to present names and characteristics;
it cannot be taken as something rigid,
for this is a name from the past.
Furthermore, an objection is raised:
"Since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cannot apprehend an object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
how can there be a past object that was previously perceived?"
Answer: Both types are designated as being in the past;
however, within them there is a distinction between those that proceed alone and those that proceed without contact.
Furthermore, it was asked:
Since both types of names and characteristics are all deluded consciousness,
the Sūtra asks:
"How could there be a solitary image?"
There are images that possess a substrate.

To the question of what it means for an image to "possess a substrate," the answer is: such an image is also a "solitary shadow" (duoying) perceived by the mind; because it takes the specific characteristics of an object as its basis, it is an object of inference (anumāna), and therefore not a direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Therefore, it is now explained separately;
it is explained separately because the common eye-consciousness is not uncommon [to all].
Furthermore, he asked:
Question: Why are the types of discrimination not the same? Answer:
Because there is discrimination that is manifest and discrimination that is retentive.
There are two kinds of differences.
Therefore, there are those that rely on a physical substrate and those that do not rely on a physical substrate.
This is because their conceptualizations differ.
The deluded person asked again:
"I see only two kinds of names and characteristics."
"What dharma do you, O wise one, perceive?
He replied,
"The wise person perceives only the dharma of form."
One does not perceive names or marks.
This concludes the exclusion of names.
Next, as for entering the gate of non-arising:
Now, when a wise person contemplates the dharma of form: for instance,
when the visual consciousness apprehends a form, there is in fact no discrimination.
It is not that there is no discrimination because nothing is apprehended;
rather, this is the dharmadhātu-consciousness directly realizing suchness as being non-different from form.
When the mental consciousness fails to understand this, it falsely conceives of a self.
Birth arises from false discrimination;
through inverted views, one sinks into the cycle of existence.
Within the phenomena of the mundane world, the true and the false reach a state of equilibrium.
What is it that the mental consciousness discriminates as not in accordance with the Dharma?
Regarding what is called "the true and the false":
because it is apprehended by the visual consciousness, it is termed "true."
Because consciousness functions through conditions, it is false;
true reality is suspended from this in its distinctions and inequalities.
Therefore, in the realization of the Dharma, there is no person.
Why is this? Because dharmas are without discrimination.
As the Sūtra says:
Dharmas are without discrimination;
if one engages in discrimination,
that itself is discrimination.
This is not seeking the Dharma.
As it is with the dharmas of form,
so it is with the dharmas of mind.
Judging by this through reflection,
it is no different from form;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
The objects apprehended by the five consciousnesses are, in their very essence, the Tathāgatagarbha and so forth.
This is the expedient means for entering the initial gate;
it is the wondrous door that accords with one's own station.
The general meaning is explained in brief as such;
a detailed exposition is as set forth in the sūtras and śāstras.
Furthermore, all phenomena are entirely characterized by emptiness, without exception.
Within this, there are further two contemplations:
first, the contemplation of non-arising;
second, the contemplation of signlessness.
Regarding what is called the contemplation of non-arising:
phenomena have no intrinsic nature;
they arise through dependence upon conditions.
Birth is not substantially existent;
this is emptiness. Emptiness is without even the slightest trace.
Therefore it is said that there is no arising.
As the Sūtra says:
"By way of causes and conditions, things exist."
"It is empty because it lacks intrinsic nature.
The commentary explains:
"Lacking intrinsic nature" refers to dependent origination.
Conditions are themselves without intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"Because emptiness exists..."
All phenomena are thereby established.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"If all phenomena were not empty..."
Thus, there is neither path nor fruit, and so forth.
Second, as for the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*):
signs are themselves signless.
Why is this? Because phenomena are devoid of marks.
As the Sūtra says:
Dharmas are free from marks because they have no objective referent.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
All phenomena are empty;
they possess not even a trace of characteristics.
Emptiness is devoid of conceptual differentiation.
As stated in the *Ākāśagarbha-dvāra-śāstra*:
"Even the dharma of non-nature does not exist,
for all things are empty."
Because one contemplates these phenomena as being free from emotional attachment, it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
Question: All phenomena are empty.
How is contemplation established?
Answer: It is precisely because all phenomena are empty that contemplation can be established.
If it were not empty,
it would be a perversion; how, then,
could it constitute contemplation?
Question: For one who practices such contemplation, what kind of illness is being treated?
Answer: It treats the illness of clinging to superior dharmas.
Why is this? Phenomena are in reality non-existent;
they are seen as existent through delusion.
Due to false views,
one then claims that true suchness and nirvana can be attained,
and that birth-and-death and conditioned phenomena can be abandoned.
Because of this view,
it constitutes a sickness;
now one knows that all phenomena are empty.
As it is in accordance with the Dharma and free from error,
one achieves contemplation.
Thus, a sutra says:
Suchness and the dharma-realm,
enlightenment and the limit of reality,
as well as the various types of mind-born bodies.
I have taught that these are equivalent to the "mind-only" (cittamātra).
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Because it is non-conceptual emptiness, it is called contemplation."
All dharmas are empty in their nature; there is nothing that does not reach this exhaustion.
I have briefly set forth these fundamental principles;
you should reflect upon them accordingly.
The former gate yields the wisdom of the selflessness of persons;
this initial-stage Bodhisattva thus attains the two-fold emptiness of both person and phenomena,
which is also termed the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena.
The Third: The Contemplation of the Perfect Interfusion of Phenomena and Principle. Regarding this contemplation of the perfect interfusion of phenomena and principle, there are further two gates.
The first is the gate of the suchness of mind;
the second is the gate of the arising and ceasing of mind.
The gate of the suchness of mind refers to principle.
The arising and ceasing of the mind is a matter of fact;
it refers precisely to the two views of emptiness and existence,
which are sovereign and perfectly interfused.
Though their manifestations of concealment and appearance differ,
they ultimately encounter no obstruction.
To say there is "no duality" means:
The phenomena of dependent origination appear to exist yet are empty;
being empty, they are not empty,
and thus they once again become existent.
Existence and emptiness are non-dual;
they are a single limit of perfect fusion,
wherein the two views have perished.
Emptiness and existence are unimpeded. Why is this?
Because truth and delusion reflect one another, encompassing all things through and through.
Why is this? Emptiness is the emptiness that does not obstruct existence;
it is eternally present within emptiness itself.
There is this existence that does not obstruct emptiness;
because it is existent while being eternally empty,
existence is itself non-existence.
When existence is free from the extreme of existence,
emptiness is itself non-empty;
when emptiness is free from the extreme of non-existence, it is so.
Emptiness and existence are perfectly interfused as one without duality;
therefore, emptiness and existence do not obstruct one another.
Because they mutually negate and transcend each other, both extremes are simultaneously left behind.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"One who deeply penetrates dependent origination severs all false views;
regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence, no further habitual tendencies remain."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"By means of causes and conditions, phenomena arise;
by means of causes and conditions, phenomena cease."
If one can understand in this way,
such a person will swiftly attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
The profound Tathāgatagarbha is always accompanied by the seven consciousnesses;
it gives rise to two kinds of appropriation.
The wise, however, remain far removed from them.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"To be stained yet unstained."
It is difficult to comprehend.
To be unstained yet stained is difficult to comprehend.
Based on this meaning,
it is possible for calm abiding and insight to proceed together, with compassion and wisdom guiding one another. Why is this so?
Because existence is identical to emptiness and yet not existent, it is called "stopping" (śamatha).
Because emptiness is identical to existence and yet not empty, it is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
Since emptiness and existence are fully integrated as non-dual yet dual, it is both stopping and contemplation.
Because emptiness and existence mutually negate one another yet are non-dual, they are neither cessation nor contemplation.
As for the statement that "compassion and wisdom guide each other," it means that while existence is precisely emptiness, existence is not lost.
Compassion guides wisdom so that one does not dwell in emptiness;
for emptiness is itself existence, yet emptiness is not lost.
Wisdom guides compassion so that one does not stagnate in existence.
Because of his great compassion that does not abide in emptiness,
he constantly follows the realm of existence to gather in sentient beings; yet,
because he does not grasp at gathering in sentient beings, [he remains free].
Because of the great wisdom that does not stagnate in existence,
one constantly dwells in emptiness without realizing cessation;
this cessation is the cessation of non-cessation.
Cessation is non-cessation;
arising is the arising of non-arising; birth is non-birth.
Because arising is not [truly] arising,
the characteristic of arising is turbulent yet non-existent.
Because cessation is not [truly] ceasing...
The dharma of the mark of emptiness is yet not empty;
because the dharma of the mark of emptiness is yet not empty,
saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are brought together as one.
The characteristics of birth are chaotic and yet non-existent;
therefore, nirvana and samsara are not distinct. Why is this?
Because emptiness and existence are a perfect fusion that is both one and not one,
they may also be analyzed into four propositions;
for existence is itself emptiness.
One does not abide in saṃsāra,
because emptiness is itself existence;
one does not abide in nirvāṇa.
Because emptiness and existence both exist simultaneously,
one dwells both in saṃsāra and in nirvāṇa;
because emptiness and existence mutually cancel each other out, neither exists.
It dwells neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa;
it is illustrated by the metaphor of water and waves.
The mutual relation of high and low constitutes the wave.
The equality of moisture is water;
waves are not different from water.
By means of the waves, one clarifies the water.
Water is not different from the water of the waves;
it is precisely water that constitutes the waves.
Waves and water are one, yet they do not obstruct their distinctness.
The waves are distinct yet do not obstruct the one;
because they do not obstruct the one, that which dwells in the water is itself the waves.
Because they do not obstruct their distinctness, that which dwells in the waves constantly abides in the water.
Why is this? Because water and waves are both distinct and not distinct.
As the sutra says:
Sentient beings are themselves the mark of nirvāṇa and do not undergo further extinction;
they also attain nirvāṇa which is itself the nature of sentient beings and does not undergo further rebirth.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
The Tathāgata perceives neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa;
saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal and without distinction.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
Within the unconditioned realm, the conditioned realm is manifest,
yet it does not destroy the nature of the unconditioned;
the same applies equally to the conditioned realm.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"It is not the practice of ordinary beings;
it is not the practice of noble sages."
"This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
The commentary explains:
"Ordinary beings who practice cling to existence."
The practitioner of the noble path abides in non-existence.
Now, there is both existence and non-existence;
they are non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual.
Therefore, one simultaneously departs from both errors and abruptly severs all hundred negations;
the seeing-mind finds no place of reliance.
Therefore, it is called "contemplation" (*guan*).
The fourth section, the Gate of the Dual Extinction of Speech and Contemplation: As for the dual extinction of speech and contemplation, it is as the Sūtra says:
"The path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished."
Thus, regarding the two aforementioned gates of emptiness and existence,
one transcends the sphere of all discursive speech and mental activity;
there remains only suchness and the wisdom of suchness.
Why is this? Because the perfect fusion of phenomena mutually subsumes all marks,
and whatever thoughts arise are immediately identical to suchness.
Because there is ultimately no subject or object, nor this or that;
it alone seizes and reveals that defilement is not a thing.
As the Sūtra says:
"Only suchness and the wisdom of suchness remain," and so forth.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The quiescent mark of all phenomena cannot be expressed in words."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The Dharma is free from all modes of contemplative practice.
Another sutra states:
If one understands the ultimate reality, there is no bodhi.

Question: If it is said that emptiness and existence are perfectly interfused and that both speech and contemplation are transcended, does this not mean one is detached from the practice of contemplation?
How does one realize and enter [this state]?
The answer is: it is not a matter of remaining silent and saying nothing;
rather, it is because speech itself is suchness.
It is not different from the Dharma;
therefore, it is ineffable.
Contemplative practice is likewise so.
The opposite of the above can be understood accordingly.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
"There are thirty-two bodhisattvas."
Each spoke of duality as non-duality and non-duality as duality;
this is called "entering the gate of the non-dual Dharma.
Next, they came to Vimalakīrti.
He answered silently, remaining in a state of wordless stillness;
this is called truly entering the Dharma-door of non-duality.
Mañjuśrī praised him, saying:
Excellent, excellent!
To remain silent and without speech is the true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
The commentary states:
Although Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no words,
this itself was the teaching of the Dharma.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas have attained liberation.
What does this mean?
It is said that the contemplation of verbal discourse is itself the Dharma.
One might ask: since emptiness and existence are non-dual, how can it cause the Mahāsattva to be without words?
Since essence and characteristics are fused, how can it leave the contemplating mind with no place to rest?
I believe it is as you have said.
However, I do not yet understand by what skillful means those who practice today realize and accord with this truth.
Answer: One discerns and grasps it precisely within this very emptiness that possesses phenomena. Why is this so?
By means of emptiness, one subsumes existence;
thus existence is not existence,
and the view of existence is exhausted.
By means of existence, one encompasses emptiness;
thus, emptiness is not [merely] empty.
When attachment to emptiness is entirely extinguished, [true emptiness is realized].
When emptiness and existence are present, one immediately enters the state where the whole body interpenetrates.
There is but a single phase without duality, and the two views do not arise.
This interpenetration is unimpeded; though there is obstruction, it does not obstruct, and both aspects coexist.
Mutually subsuming yet perfectly interfusing, they do not abolish either side, nor are both simultaneously extinguished.
Thus, by attaining the perfect pearl, one is sovereign and need not be constrained by various views;
by realizing the ocean of nature, one is beyond reproach.
Tranquil and beyond all things, transcending emotion and departing from thought;
far exceeding the reach of deliberation, it suddenly blocks out all that is wrong.
Both speech and contemplation are utterly severed.
Thus, the deluded mind is made to melt away like ice and all views are stripped away like clouds;
there is only the realization of direct correspondence,
which has nothing to do with verbal expression.
Thus, Vimalakīrti’s silent response was intended to demonstrate that the ultimate principle transcends the starting point of words;
the goddess’s eloquent discourse was intended to show that the true nature is not outside of words.
That the true nature is not outside of words—
Speech is itself non-speech;
principle emerges from the source of words.
Not speaking is itself speaking.
Because non-speaking is itself speaking,
it transcends the conceptual deliberations of the intellect;
because speaking is itself non-speaking, it is beyond words.
To utterly dissolve the mind’s scheming deliberations and thereby harmonize and transcend them—
how could this ever be fully expressed through the brush?
It can only be realized through personal experience;
one must know it for oneself.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
It is like a person drinking cold water who knows it only for themselves;
this meaning lies beyond words.
Do not cling to the literal expression or conceptual reasoning.
Principle does not lie outside of words;
do not discard words in search of principle.
Thoroughly understand and investigate their subtle nuances.
Furthermore, it is already manifest;
having been polished with meticulous care,
it ought to be clear indeed.
One must simply apply diligent effort with undivided focus,
ensuring that practice is not abandoned for even a moment during walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; by practicing thus without ceasing for a long time, [the goal will be attained].
It is deeply credible that white and black are distinct from one another;
thus, a sutra says:
"It is like a person who, being thirsty, requires water."
One drills and excavates at a high plateau;
if one applies effort without ceasing,
one will gradually encounter moist soil.
One knows that water must be near.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"It is like a person drilling for fire who stops before the heat has been generated."
The intensity of the fire subsides and is extinguished accordingly;
so it is with those who are indolent.
Furthermore, the treatise says:
It is like a person dreaming of crossing a river who awakens by the power of their own vigor;
if one's application of effort is interrupted, [the same result follows].
As soon as one acts, it ceases;
seeking awakening, one will ultimately find it difficult to expect.
Hoping for understanding, the years and months pass in vain.
Why is this? Because the defilements of beginningless karmic habits are heavy and difficult to pierce;
thus, although one possesses an awakened mind, [it remains obscured].
As soon as it is seen, it is extinguished.
If one does not apply oneself with diligent earnestness,
there is no way to perfect the mind of practice.
Following the sun, they falsely take this to be their concern;
they merely exhaust their own physical strength in vain.
Indeed, the practitioner should maintain mindfulness of this.

The Fifth Gate: The Flower Adornment Samādhi. Regarding this fifth gate of the Flower Adornment Samādhi, those who are deluded about the dependent origination of the Dharma-realm find it difficult to ascend.
If one has not first washed away the defiled mind, [one cannot enter].
Without this, one cannot attain perfect enlightenment.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"It is like a person who has excrement beneath their nose; though they smell the stench,"
Even fragrances such as agarwood and musk are considered foul.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"Do not use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to explain the Dharma of the true mark."
One must first establish a conceptual framework;
only then may one enter perfect luminosity.
If there is direct insight that all phenomena, such as form and so forth, arise from conditions.
This is precisely the dependent origination of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-pratītyasamutpāda).
It is not necessary to further employ preliminary expedients (pūrvayoga).
Should one be unable to enter directly into this, [one must rely on them].

One should interrogate [the student] point by point from beginning to end, ensuring that delusions are severed and confusion exhausted, so that the Dharma transcends words, the nature of reality is perceived, and understanding arises; only then can one be said to have attained the essential meaning.
Question:
How is it that by seeing all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*),
one immediately enters the great *dharmadhātu* of dependent origination?
The answer is:
Because phenomena such as form are fundamentally and truly beyond verbal expression,
they are inaccessible to the deluded mind.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Verbal expressions are provisional applications;
reality is beyond words."
Therefore, when one perceives phenomena such as the eyes and ears,
one immediately enters into the dharmadhātu of dependent origination. Why is this?
All these lack substantial reality;
they are established precisely through the illusory appearance of non-substantiality,
because they arise from conditions and do not exist by way of their own nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, through the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one realizes illusory existence.
Therefore, essence and characteristics are thoroughly fused and entirely encompassed within a single limit.
Consequently, upon seeing phenomena, one immediately enters the great *dharmadhātu* of dependent origination.

Question: Since it has already been stated that realizing the non-duality of emptiness and existence constitutes entry into interpenetration, why is it further said that seeing the eyes, ears, and so forth constitutes entry into the Dharma-realm?
Answer: If one can see emptiness and existence in such a manner, [then it is so].
Only when false views and the mind are exhausted can one accord with principle and enter the Dharma-realm.
Why is this? Because the Dharma-realm of dependent origination is free from views and the loss of sentiment, yet gives rise to the myriad phenomena in profusion.
Question: Since one already knows it to be thus, by what skillful means can one cause entry?
Answer: Skillful means are diverse; briefly, there are three kinds.
First is the method of interrogation to see the ultimate limit.
This is like questioning by pointing to a specific object, asking, "What is this eye?
as was previously done in the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) through six kinds of analysis.
If all phenomena are subsumed within the gateway of "mere names," such that there is not a single phenomenon that is not a name,
one must further inquire into the reason for knowing that the eye and so forth are indeed names.
In this manner, one successively interrogates the reasons for [the opponent's positions] until they are rendered speechless and their interpretations are cut off.
Second, one demonstrates the Dharma to induce reflection.
This further consists of two sections.
First, the stripping away of the perverted mind;
once this is exhausted, it is as explained in the section on "pointing out the object."
By means of visible forms, fragrances, tastes, tangibles,
and so forth, one seizes away their false conceptualizations and causes them to realize their delusions and inversions.
All grasping that is contrary to the Dharma is produced by the habitual perfuming of beginningless false views of the mental consciousness; since beginningless time,
it has been dragged along with urgency, continuing to be born within the three realms.
The cycle continues without interruption.
If one can awaken to the knowledge that this grasping is itself dependent origination,
it is unborn in its very place.
Second, the teaching of the Dharma to sever attachment:
if one does not first recognize the deluded mind before the Dharma is taught,
it will instead result in inverted confusion.
If one does not demonstrate the Dharma so that they may see it,
their deluded mind will revert to clinging to emptiness;
therefore, one first strips away the deluded mind.
Subsequently, he manifests the Dharma so that it may be seen.
Third, he reveals that the Dharma transcends speech and is beyond conceptual understanding.
Within this section, there are also two parts.
First, the negation of conceptual attachment;
second, the manifestation of virtue.
Regarding the negation of conceptual attachment:
Question: Is dependent origination existent?
Answer: No, because it is empty.
The dharmas of dependent origination are without intrinsic nature and are thus empty.
Question: Is this non-existence? Answer: No.
Question: Since it exists, and because the phenomena of dependent origination exist precisely by virtue of being beginningless, does it both exist and not exist? Answer: No.
Because emptiness and existence are perfectly interfused as one and not two;
for the phenomena of dependent origination have a single limit where emptiness and existence meet, being without dual characteristics.
Consider this, for example, like gold and its ornaments.
Question: Is it neither existent nor non-existent?
Answer: No, because there is no obstruction to the coexistence of both.
Because, according to the principle of dependent origination, emptiness and existence mutually negate one another while simultaneously establishing one another.
Question: Is it definitively non-existent? Answer: No.
Because emptiness and existence are mutually integrated and neither remains,
when the dharma of dependent origination is subsumed by emptiness, existence is exhausted and there is only emptiness,
not existence; when existence subsumes emptiness, emptiness is exhausted and there is only existence, not emptiness.
When they are simultaneously sublated, both aspects vanish together.
Regarding the two manifestations of virtue:
one asks, "Is dependent origination existent?"
Answer: It is so.
Because that which is illusory exists and is not non-existent.
Question: Is it then non-existent?
Answer: It is so.
This is because that which lacks intrinsic nature is itself emptiness.
Question: Is it both existent and non-existent?
Answer: It is so.
For there is no obstruction to their coexistence.
Question: Is it neither existent nor non-existent?
The answer is yes.
This is because they mutually negate one another and thus both vanish;
furthermore, they exist by virtue of dependent origination.
Because it arises through dependent origination, it is non-existent;
because it arises through dependent origination, it is both existent and non-existent;
because it arises through dependent origination, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Even unto "one," "not one," "both one and not one," and "neither one nor not one."
Many, not many; both many and not many;
neither many nor not many.
Thus, it is many;
it is one;
and it is both many and one.
It is neither one nor many;
the four propositions of "is" and "is not" are to be understood accordingly.
This is because the interpenetration of negation and affirmation is perfectly harmonious and unimpeded, all arising from the sovereign nature of dependent origination.
If one can do so, only then will one be able to perceive the dharma of dependent origination. Why is this?
Because it is called "seeing according to the Dharma" when all aspects are perfectly interfused and of one limit;
if one does not see them as identical before and after,
that is a perverted view and not the correct view.
Why is this? Because seeing things as distinct before and after does not accord with the Dharma.
Having asked thus: "What is seen in this way?"
How does one enter the dharma-dhātu through skillful means?
The answer is: that which is called "entering through skillful means" refers to [entering] within the context of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
The message is derived from this:
that is to say,
these very phenomena of dependent origination are themselves empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.
Because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), illusory existence is established;
yet this phenomenon takes precisely the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature as its very essence.
Therefore, this phenomenon is itself the absence of intrinsic nature, and yet it does not obstruct the persistence of its appearances.
If there were no absence of intrinsic nature,
dependent origination would not be established,
because that which is devoid of intrinsic nature does not arise, as all things arise from conditions.
Since it fully encompasses all natures to their ultimate extent,
nature itself is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and beyond conceptual differentiation.
Whether great or small, there is no nature that is not perfectly complete within it.
All things are likewise the body of the whole nature;
therefore, the whole is this.
Thus, the nature itself does not obstruct illusory appearances.
Therefore, the one encompasses the many.
Since each is entirely contained within the other,
their mutual distinctness is not obstructed.
Therefore, that exists within this,
and this exists within that.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
The Dharma is identical to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
because it enters into all phenomena.
To explain:
"Dharma" refers to the phenomena that are dependently originated and illusorily existent.
"Of the same nature" means that dependent origination is itself emptiness, yet it does not obstruct these phenomenal marks.
The entirety of that is fully subsumed within this,
because that is itself emptiness and does not obstruct its own appearance.
Since this and that are fully subsumed, their respective characteristics remain unimpaired.
Therefore, this contains that,
and that contains this;
it is not merely a matter of mutual containment between them.
All things are likewise so.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Within one, understand the immeasurable."
Within the immeasurable, one is understood;
these arise successively and are not real.
The wise have nothing to fear.
It is further said:
"Within a single dharma, one understands manifold dharmas;
within manifold dharmas, one understands a single dharma."
In this manner, they mutually encompass one another and thus enter into each other;
they manifest simultaneously and instantaneously, without before or after.
According to any single [aspect], there is perfect interfusion, such that it entirely encompasses both itself and the other.
Question: Since the Dharma is thus, how is wisdom?
Answer: Wisdom accords with the Dharma.
Formed through conditions at a single limit,
it is in profound resonance without distinction;
though it manifests instantaneously, there is no absence of sequence.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The realm of the Universal Eye is the pure body;
I shall now expound it—let all people listen attentively."
The commentary states:
"The Universal Eye" refers to the simultaneous manifestation of many dharmas through correspondence with the wisdom of dharmas (*dharmajñāna*).
This clarifies that the Dharma is known only by the wisdom of the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*), distinguishing it from the domain of other forms of wisdom.
"Domain" refers here to the Dharma itself.
It clarifies that many dharmas interpenetrate one another, like the infinite, layered realms of Indra’s net or celestial jewels.

As for the "pure body," this clarifies that the aforementioned dharmas simultaneously enter into one another; their beginning and end are difficult to trace, and they are seen as a collection of dependent origination, with the perceiving mind having no place of reliance.
Now, as for the pearl net of Śakra-devānām-indra,
it is called the Indra-net (Indrājāla).
Furthermore, this celestial net is composed entirely of jewels.
Because the jewels are luminous and transparent, they reflect one another in successive layers of mutual penetration;
within a single jewel, all appear simultaneously and instantaneously,
and it is the same for each and every one.
In truth, there is ultimately no coming or going.
For now, let us go toward the southwestern border and take a single pearl to test this.
This single jewel can instantaneously manifest the reflections of all jewels;
as it is with this jewel,
so it is with every other one.
Since all the jewels appear simultaneously within each individual jewel,
and this is so for every one of them, so it is for all others as well;
thus, they are layered upon one another without limit or boundary.
Within this very finite [jewel], there are successively infinite jewel-reflections,
all clearly and loftily manifest within a single jewel;
none of the others obstruct this.
If one sits within a single jewel,
one is simultaneously seated within all the jewels of the ten directions,
layer upon layer. Why is this?
Because within a single jewel there are all jewels,
when there is a single jewel within all jewels,
one is also simultaneously wearing all jewels.
All things are the opposite of this;
consider it by analogy with reflection.
Since one has already entered all jewels within a single jewel, [the same applies to all others].
Yet, in the end, this single jewel does not emerge;
all jewels enter into this one jewel,
yet this single jewel never arises.
Question: Since it is said that one enters all jewels within a single jewel yet does not emerge from this single jewel, how can one enter all jewels?
Answer: It is precisely because one does not emerge from this jewel.
Therefore, one attains entry into all jewels.
If, upon emerging from this single jewel, one enters all jewels, then one does not truly enter all jewels. Why is this?
Because there is no other jewel apart from within this jewel.
Question: If there are no jewels whatsoever apart from within this jewel, then this net would be merely [this single jewel].
If it is formed from a single jewel, how can you say that many jewels are joined together to form it?
Answer: It is precisely because there is only a single jewel that one then joins many together to form a net.
Why is this? Because it is by means of this single jewel alone that the net is formed;
if this jewel were removed, [the net would cease to exist].
Because there is no net at all.
Question: If there is only a single jewel, how can it be said that a net is formed?
Answer: Regarding the statement that "a net is formed by many pearls," it refers to a single pearl alone. Why is this so?
First, because the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) is established through the aggregation of many;
for if there were not even one,
there would be nothing at all.
Therefore, this net is formed by a single jewel;
all enter into one.
This can be understood through reflection.
Question: Although a single jewel at the southwestern edge encompasses all jewels of the ten directions exhaustively without remainder,
and yet there are jewels in each direction individually,
why do you say that the net is formed by only a single jewel?
The answer is that all the jewels of the ten directions are,
in fact, a single jewel from the southwest direction. Why is this so?
The single jewel in the southwest direction is, in fact, all the jewels of the ten directions.
If one does not believe that the single jewel in the southwest direction is identical to all the jewels of the ten directions, [then...]
If one merely applies a dot of ink to a single bead on the southwestern side,
as soon as that one bead is marked, every bead throughout the ten directions will bear a dot of ink.
Since every pearl throughout the ten directions has a black dot upon it,
we know that all the pearls of the ten directions are, in fact, a single pearl.
To say that the pearls of the ten directions are not the same as the single pearl on the southwestern side is [to speak erroneously].
How could this person possibly mark all the pearls throughout the ten directions at once?
Even if they were to mark every single pearl throughout the ten directions,
it would still be but a single pearl.
Since this is the case for the first instance,
it is likewise for all others; thus,
layer upon layer without end, every single point is identical.
Profound and difficult to trace to their origin,
once completed, all is finished.
Contemplate this wondrous analogy as being analogous to the Dharma.
The Dharma is not like that;
the analogy is no different from a non-analogy,
for it is spoken of only because of a partial similarity.
Why is this? This jewel merely receives the reflected image;
its substance remains distinct from that of the original object.
The Dharma is not like that,
for its entire substance is mutually pervasive.
As the "Nature-Arising" Chapter of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings and causing them all to attain understanding and liberation,
the true meaning is revealed through non-analogies.
Such a subtle and esoteric Dharma is difficult to hear even in immeasurable kalpas.
Those possessing diligence and wisdom hear of the *tathāgatagarbha*, as it is said in the sutras:
"Using that which is not a metaphor as a metaphor," and so forth.
All practitioners should reflect upon this according to the metaphors provided.
The past practices of Vairocana Buddha have caused the oceans of buddha-fields to be entirely purified—
immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless. In all those places,
the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is sovereign and pervasive, inconceivable, formless, signless, and without peer.
Manifesting physical forms for the sake of sentient beings, he appears everywhere throughout the ten directions where there are those to be transformed.
Within every atom of all Buddha-fields, Vairocana manifests his sovereign power;
with the ocean-like resonance of his great vows, he tames all classes of sentient beings.
The *Brief Record of the Venerable Dushun of Huayan* concludes.
The *Origins of Chan Master Dushun of Zhongnan Mountain*. Regarding the origins of Chan Master Dushun of Zhongnan Mountain: this Chan Master had a disciple.
He served him for more than thirty years.
His disciple was constantly thinking of going to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; one day, he suddenly consulted his Upādhyāya regarding this matter.
"I, your disciple, wish to travel to Mount Wutai to pay my respects.
I pray that the Upādhyāya, out of compassion, will permit me to go.
Although the Upādhyāya repeatedly and earnestly tried to detain him, he could not be persuaded to stay.
The Chan master then released him, saying,
"Go now, but return early;
I shall wait for you."
He then took his leave of the Upādhyāya;
after traveling for ten months, he finally arrived at Mount Wutai,
where he paid homage with sincere devotion.
Suddenly he encountered an old man who asked,
"From where have you come?
The disciple replied:
"I have come from Mount Zhongnan.
For what purpose have you come?
I have come specifically to pay homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva."
The old man said,
"Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is not here.
The disciple asked the old man:
"Where is he? The old man replied,
"He is at Mount Zhongnan."
The Chan Master Dushun was that person.
His disciples were astonished and informed the old man, saying,
"This disciple has served his Upādhyāya for thirty years."
The old man said,
"Although you have served me,
you have never known me."
"You must return immediately; if you arrive at nightfall, you will see him, but if you stay overnight, you will not.
You can go right now and succeed."
That man was most extraordinary;
he set out a month ago and has now returned today.
"If you wish to seek lodging, you may go there.
Believing these words of the old man,
he immediately turned back and arrived at the Western Capital in a short while.
As the sun was already low in the evening, he found it most strange;
he then proceeded to visit the houses of various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*),
yet they were all not at home for a short while.
Just as the sound of the drum struck,
he intended to rush out through the south gate,
but it had already been closed.
Deeply regretting that he could not leave the city,
he returned to the house of his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and stayed there for the night. At dawn, he set out.
He immediately left the city and traveled swiftly to the mountain,
only to find that the Upādhyāya had already entered parinirvāṇa the previous night.
The man was filled with profound resentment.
I may not see my Upādhyāya again;
I am overcome with such bitter grief and sobbing.
It is just as the Old Man of Wutai said.
Only then did he realize it was Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.

The Chan Master’s commentaries on the *Huayan fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Huayan Dharma-realm), the *Shixuan zhiguan yi hai* (The Ocean of Meaning of the Ten Mysterious Gates of Stopping and Contemplation),
and other works are still practiced in the world today.
This was none other than a transformation body of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
